MORE DEVILTRY.
An Attempt at Robbery and Assassination at Chillicothe.
Chillicothe, Mo., June 11, 2 p.m. —
This morning at 4 o'clock, a supposed attempt was made to rob the ticket office of the Hannibal and St. Joseph railroad at this place, by a party of negroes, whose depredations upon public and private property are becoming to frequent to be much longer endured by a civilized community. At the hour named a number of these characters had congregated at the stock pen, nearly opposite from the depot, while two of their number were appointed to begin their devilish work Henry Smith, night operator, had just opened the ticket office, which is located about twenty feet from the telegraph office and north of the passenger waiting room, while Fred Tucker, the night assistant, was left in charge of the instruments. Approaching the door one of them urged the other, in loud words, to "go in and send the dispatch." Entering, he asked one or two common place questions and then, with an oath, drew a revolver and fired, the ball entering the right cheek near the corner of the mouth and coming out back of the ear. Tucker was seated in a chair at the time this shot was fired and jumped to catch the assassin, who ran out on the platform. Closing the door, Tucker wheeled around to get his revolver, and in doing so, was in the act of raising his right hand to the wound when the accomplice fired at him through the window, the shot taking effect at the second joint of the thumb, the ball lodging near the wrist joint and disabling him from using a revolver. Parties near the depot, hearing the firing, hurried to the scene of conflict, which frightened the gang away and probably prevented any further attempt at life or property. Mr. Tucker is one of the finest young men in the city, and his friends, to the number of 100 or more, including city and county officials, are in close pursuit of these thieves and assassins. Tucker's wounds are not dangerous.

CRIME RAMPANT. TWO NEGROES, WITH MURDER AND ROBBERY IN THEIR HEARTS, SHOOT A TELEGRAPH OPERATOR AT A CHILLICOTHE RAILROAD DEPOT. AND ARE CAUGHT AFTER AN EXCITING CHASE AND LODGED IN JAIL, JUST IN TIME TO SAVE THEIR NECKS. A MOB OF 100 MEN CALL FOR THEM AT THE DEAD HOUR OF MIDNIGHT. BUT OUR BRAVE SHERIFF MANTAINS THE SUPREMACY OF THE LAW.
Sunday morning about 3:45 o'clock, two young negro men, Alex Murray and Charles Shelby, entered the H. & St. Joe telegraph office in this city and told Fred Tucker, who was there learning telegraphy, that they wanted to send a dispatch. Tucker who was in a recining position on the table and was in a doze, answered, "all right, write it out," and thinking they were joking, did not get up. The negroes went out but Murray come back in a few minutes and saying "get up you —," pulled a revolver and shot Tucker in the face the ball entering near the mouth and coming out just below the ear on the same side. Tucker jumped up and called for Henry Smith who was in the ticket office, when Shelby fired through

from the second shot, and was received when he put his hand on his wounded cheek, but from an examination of the telegraph office and the course of the two shots, it is thought that the first shot must have inflicted both wounds, which could easily have been done if he was resting on his elbow. The alarm was given and Fred was accompanied to his hotel, the Marcum House. By ten o'clock dozens of men were scouring the country south and east of town. George Graham and Policeman Tom Anderson got on the track of Shelby and in the afternoon overhauled him in Linn county, about two and a half miles north of Meadville and 12 or 13 miles east of here. They brought him back, took him to the Marcum House where he was clearly identified by Tucker, and then hastened with him to the jail, arriving there less than a minute ahead of a large and excited crowd.

The search for Murray was continued and about supper time he was found in an empty house in north-west part of town just across the street from his mother's residence. W. T. Folwell, Wallace Brown and L. S. Bearce entered the house through a window and discovered Murray asleep on the floor. Folwell grabbed his hands, Wallace Brown seized his feet and Bearce grabbed him by the arms. His pistol was taken from him and he was hurried to the jail as it was known two ropes were taken out there by some of the searchers.

THE SHERIFF'S NIGHT CALLERS.

About 1 o'clock, Sunday night, about 100 men called at the jail and demanded Murray and Shelby. In the jail were Sherin Leeper, his wife and his sons, Dr. Carl Leeper, of Catawba, and Willie Leeper. They were all upstairs, but the sheriff, who was down stairs in the south east room. He raised the window, threw open the shutters and calmly reasoned with his callers and at the same time informed them that he would kill the first man who attempted to enter the door. About this time the street lamp was shot out and one near the sheriff fired his pistol in the air. Most of the crowd thinking Leeper fired the shot, fled precipitately. The others soon dispersed and everything was quiet the remainder of the night.

THEY STOLE FOUR HORSES or at least that is the supposition. On Saturday night two horses were stolen at Utica from F. Bonderer and two from Green Cooper at the Water Tank between here and Utica. Sunday morning, Geo. Hoskins residing this side of the river and near the Spring Hill road, started to his barn to feed his horses when two negroes came out and shot at him and decamped after Hoskins had snapped a shot gun at them.

Park Giltner Sunday morning about 7:30 while on his way to a pasture just north of town, saw Alex Murray coming in from the country, but not knowing he was wanted paid no attention to him.

The horses were all recovered Sunday. Two in the bottom west of town and the other two on the Spring Hill road in the vicinity of J. H. Abshire's. So it is pretty certain that Murray and Snelby with perhaps some accomplices stole the horses. A colored man by the name of Hampton Arnold has been arrested on suspicion of being one of the thieves and is now in jail. The revolver found on Murray when arrested is one which was stolen from Henry Leeper's hardware store a few nights ago.

Murray and Shelby are not strangers in our jail. Murray has been in the penitentiary; was tried in January for burglarizing Fowler's saloon and was acquitted, the evidence being slight, but subsequent events proved him guilty. He is the son of Sarah Bryan who was a slave of the late Thomas Bryan. His brother George was hung in the southern suburbs of th is city about 9 years ago by a vigilance committee from south of the river for outraging a little girl.

Shelby was tried at the recent session of Circuit Court for stealing a pocket book and money from Gus. Henry's house one night last summer, but was discharged, there being no evidence of his guilt, though he was undoubtedly guilty.

THE BLACK BRUTES
Who Tried to Kill the Operator at Chillicothe are Captured.
An Attempt Made to Lynch Them.
Yesterday the BAZOO gave an account of the attempt, by some negroes at Chillicothe, a town on the H. & St. Joe, to murder the telegraph operator, a young man by the name of Fred Tucker, at an early hour.

The assault was a cold-blooded, premeditated attempt at as foul a murder as was ever conceived, utterly dastardly in its conception.

Thanks to poor marksmanship, the unsuspecting young man was not killed, though he received an ugly wound in his right cheek, and one in the thumb of his right hand.

THE REPORT OF SHOTS
at once brought quite a crowd to the depot, before whose appearance the negros fled. A party large at once formed and searched the country for the would-be assassins. Late in the afternoon one of the men was captured near Meadville by George Graham and Policeman Tom Anderson, of Chillicothe, who took their prisoner back with them. Tucker identified the man as one of the crowd who made the attack. Still later in the evening a second member of the murderous gang was captured and taken back to the scene of attack. He, too, was recognized, and was sent to join his companion in the jail. The news of the capture of the men increased the excitement in the town, and threats of lynching
and it is hardly possible that any of the men engaged in the attack could be recognized.

Next morning the excitement had, to a considerable extent, died away, and all danger of a lynching picnic is considered past. Tucker, the wounded man, is doing well and will soon be back at his duty.

The conductor on the H. & St. Joe train this morning told a different story of the attack to an Evening Star reporter. He said the man who did the shooting approached the door of the office, and seeing Tacker stretched out upon a table, deliberately fired at him without a word of warning.

Deputy Sheriff, Will Leeper, Shoots the Wrong Man.
It having been reported that Alex Murray, the colored desperado, who escaped from the penitentiary, had been seen in the vicinity of the depot, Deputies Frank Green and Will Leeper, on Thursday night watched for him at the Hannibal depot. While they were watching, a person, with a veil over his face, emerged from behind some ties near the depot and advanced on to the depot platform. Leeper ordered him to halt, which he did not do, when Leeper fired at him three times with a revolver, one shot taking effect in his abdomen. The person proved to be William Duncan, a young man who resides in this city. Duncan says he, also, was watching for Murray, in company with John Hereford, colored; that he had a shotgun, which he left on the pile of ties and came to the depot platform to watch the crowd as the train came in. He says he did not hear Leeper call halt. The wound proved to be only a flesh wound and at last accounts Duncan was rapidly recovering.

Leeper is exhonerated from blame, as he had been informed that Murray was heavily armad and had declared his intention to kill anyone who should attempt to arrest him and that he had been hiding among the piles of ties.

Richard L. Altbritain, Esq.

The numerous friends of this talented young gentleman will be deeply grieved to learn of his death about 6 o'clock this morning, at the residence of P. H. Minor, Esq. He was a son of the late Jas. Allbritain, and a grand-son of Andrew Craig. These gentlemen were early pioneers of Livingston county, and were long in the very front of our most active, usetul and honored citizens.

Richard was born and raised to manhood in this county. He was a graduate of the Normal School at Kirksville, and for a time taught school—notably, several years in the public schools of Jefferson City. During the intervals of school he read law under the advice and assistance of C. H. Mansur, Esq., of this city, and part of the time in his office. He was possessed of great energy and perseverance, and was talented in a large degree. He was the first young gentleman, under the law as it now exists, to apply to our Supreme Court for an examination, in open court, for license as an attorney, and his examination was one alike worthy of the court and of the candidate. Being admitted to the bar about three years ago, he located at Kansas City, and so great was his industry and his ability that in a twelve months he had gained a standing at that bar that made him self-supporting, and having won the affections of Miss Caddie Bolton, a most estimable young lady of Jefferson City, they were married about two years ago. No young man had a brighter future than Richard; and in his death his wife and relatives, his friends and his country, alike meet with a loss that is irreparable.

Last July, one sultry night, after being very much heated, he sat or stood in a draft, and becoming chilled, the cold settled upon his lungs, and resulted we think, from all we can learn, in a case of galloping consumption, that eventuated in his death.

Brought home, last Thursday night, by his brother William, and accompanied by his faithful and loving wife, he only returned to the scenes of his childhood and the home of his family to rapidly wither and die, like a fallen oak struck by lightning.
His remains were taken on the afternoon passenger, to-day, via Kansas City to Jefferson City, for interment. Richard L. Allbritain's generous qualities and noble nature will long keep his memory green in the minds of his many friends in Livingston county; and whose sympathy, in no unstinted measure, go out to his afflicted wife and relatives.

WHISKEY THE CAUSE OF IT.

St. Louis, March 7.—Santa Fe special: Governor Sheldon received news from Toos Pueblo yesterday, which substantiated is serious. It is to the effect that four days ago some Toos Pueblos became drunk. They were arrested and placed in jail. They escaped and deputy Sheriff Myers and Martinez started to Pueblo to re-arrest them. They and their posse were met by fifty-nine armed Pueblo Indians and a fight ensued, in which Deputy Sheriff Myers was killed and Deputy Sheriff Martinez mortally wounded. The murderers are not yet captured. The Toos Pueblos is one of the richest and largest tribes in the territory and heretofore the best of feeling has existed between the Pueblos and the surrounding Mexican towns. HORRIBLE MURDER.
Arrest and Confession of the Murderers.
Advices from Ashland, Ky., state that the murderers of the Gibbons children have been arrested on the confesssion of one of them. All live in Ashland, and two of them are married men. They are in the Cattleburg jail. Lynching is expected tonight.

A special from Ashland, Ky.. says: The three men arrested for the Gibbons murder are Wm. Neal, Ellis Craft and Geo. Ellis, all white. Ellis says Craft and Neal awakened him on the night of the murder and urged him to go with them to the Gibbons house. He went reluctantly. They entered by a window, and Neal and Craft outraged the two girls. Emma Thomas recognized Neal and said she would tell her mother. Robert, the boy, was then about to give an alarm when Craft struck him on the head with an axe, killing him instantly. Craft then told Fanny her time to die had come, and amid viteous cries of the child for mercy, he struck her on the head and killed her instantly. Neal then killed Emma Thomas in the same way. Craft and Neal at first denied Ellis' story, but Neal confessed this afternoon and both he and Ellis waived an examination. Craft will have a hearing Thursday. Ellis and Neal are married; Craft is single. They were all present when Gibbon's residence was burned and one of them drove the hearse at the funeral and another was a pall bearer. Crowds have been gathering all day at Cattlesburg and threats of lynching are common.

The Belton special to the Galveston News, republished on our first page, is strange, very strange reading. The Examiner heard, day before yesterday, that Judge Lynch had been holding court at Belton, and earnest efforts were made by this paper Monday to obtain telegraphic particulars for the Examiner of yesterday morning. We wired more than one prominent gentleman in Belton for details, but not a word came in reply, so the paper went to press silent as to the tragedy, rather than publish mere rumors. We said this dispatch is strange reading, and it is. Eight years ago when a similar ghastly scene, (but involving the murder of a far larger number of unfortunate prisoners) was enacted at Belton it was bad enough. But now it seems all but incredible that such a thing should occur. Belton is a large town now and the machinery of legal and social order is far superior to what it was eight years ago. Of course it would be manifestly unjust to hold Belton or Bell county, as a community responsible for such happenings. There is as large a proportion of good people there as anywhere in the state, and their cheeks must tinge with shame as they think of this lynching. It is very plain though that Bell county is cursed with a lawless element that would not be tolerated in any other county in the state as populous, as generally civilized as Bell. One can only feel sorrow for the good people who must loathe this devilish mob domination, and are yet powerless to shake off its rule.

Pen Pictures of the Two Victims.
Judge Lynch's recent special term of court in our sister city of Belton was a general topic of conversation yesterday, and it is hardly necessary to say the occurrence was quite generally deplored, for Belton and Bell county have strong ties on the friendship of Waco. The surprise was almost as marked as the regret, it having been supposed that with the advent of railways, telegraphs, etc., the old mob element in Bell county would become pow-rless and seek new fields and pastures green, further toward the setting sun. This latest tragedy very naturally recalled similar occurrences in the afflicted county during the past few years—such as the murder of the nine prisoners in jail in 1874; the ducking of Preacher Honey; the whipping of Dr. Russell; the strapping of the Dow brothers, etc. Said one gentleman: "I thought Belton had had her last mob. I am sorry for this, for there are good people out there and they are over-nawed by the mob element." An EXAMINER representative asked a gentleman who, until very recently has resided in Belton, if he knew the victims of Saturday night's work? "Yes," was the reply, "knew them both very well, and I cannot imagine why in the world they were lynched. Sam Shelton, the white man, was probably the most harmless man in the village. He was simply a drunken loafer, as you may see in every town, who had got in bad odor. Often accused of and tried for crookedness and meanness, he was yet never convicted, and I know that he didn't have money to give lawyers big fees, neither was his social standing of the sort to influence a jury in his favor. He was simply no account, and his chief sin seems to have been that he made an attack on a deputy sheriff out there. Jim Key, the negro, was on the same order as Shelton, loafing, hang around saloons, arrested and pay fines or work it out on the streets. Another Murder Near Ironton.
The good people of Ironton have been considerably excited on account of a murder just east of the city limits. Dr. Joseph A. Beggs was clerk at Etna Iron Works, and an eminent chemist. He was shot and killed near eleven o'clock at night, by Bill Zeck and John Wagoner. We have carefully read the testimony taken at the Coroner's inquest, as reported in the Ironton papers, and there appears to be considerable mystery about it. The case appears to be mixed up with bad women, beer and tobacco. The murderers, and the persons who were present, testify that a man came to Wagoner's house and commenced whistling and kicking against the fence. He was asked what he wanted, and what his name was. He said his name was "Old Hell." When he would not go away they shot him. There is other evidence, tending to show that the murder was committed at a point on the railroad, and not at Wagoner's house.

The citizens of Ironton have held a meeting, and passed resolutions requesting Judge Harper to hold a special term of Court to try the murderers. They also appointed a committee to raise money for the widow and children of the murdered man.

The Ironton papers speak of Dr. Beggs as a quiet, inoffensive, moral, good citizen. People sometimes differ on these questions. In Ironton, it seems, a man may spend his time and money at a beer hell until near midnight, smoking cigars and swilling beer, and yet be a model of morality in that moral city. Fanatics, like ourself, view it in a different light. In order to explain our meaning, we publish part of the testimony of two or three of the witnesses:

IRONTON, O., Jan. 20.—John Wagoner, one of the murderers of Dr. Joseph Biggs, who was shot after night on a lonesome path near the Etna Iron works nearly two months ago, was taken from the county jail by a well-organized band last night, and hanged in the court house yard. Last night for the first time in the history of Lawrence county, the slow process of the law was dispensed with, and speedy, inflexible justice administered to one murderer at least. Your readers are by this time all familiar with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, last November, an event which at the time filled this community with horror. Directly after the murder there were many threats of lynching. So many murders had been committed within the last few years in this country, and so many murderers, through the stupidity and rascality of jurors, gone unhanged, that the community and the best citizens were almost desperate. Things seemed to have reached a most dangerous state, and it was the general opinion that something radical would have to soon be done. This feeling threatened a long rope and a short shrift to the murderers.

More Lynch Law.
Our readers will remember that several weeks ago we mentioned the murder of Dr. Beggs, near Ironton. He was shot as he was going home from a saloon, about eleven o'clock at night. A man named Zeek, and another named Waggoner, were arrested and sent to jail. Zeek has made a confession, and says that Waggoner, who is his brother-in-law, did the shooting.

We believe, the way the criminal law is now not being administered, that this was right. In order to make lynch law a terror to evil-doers, it must extend, in some cases, to Judges and jurors.

Mob Law in Ohio.

John Wagoner, in jail at Ironton, Lawrence County, Ohio, charged with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, of that place, last November, was taken from jail by fifty masked men on the night of January 19 and hanged to a tree in the court-house yard. The crime of which Wagoner was guilty was a very atrocious and unprovoked one, and was committed, it has been thought, for the purpose of robbery. Dr. Beggs was a bookkeeper for an iron company, and was assaulted and murdered while on his way home from the mill, after dark had set in. Wagoner and a man named Zeek, toward whom suspicion so strongly pointed that there was little doubt remained as to their guilt, were arrested charged with the crime. On the night in question, few minutes after 12 o'clock, a knock was heard at the jail, and the Sheriff responded by opening the door. He was seized, overpowered and with cocked revolvers the mob demanded the keys of the jail. The Sheriff firmly refused, and seeing that he would not yield, he was taken into the room of his wife where the demand was repeated in a similar manner. His wife, frightened almost out of her senses, surrendered the keys, and in a moment the door to the cell in which Wagoner and Zeek were confined was swung open and the prisoners were led trembling from the cell. "I didn't mean to kill him," protested Wagoner in a tone of agony, but his words were unheeded and he was hurried into the yard and hanged without any ado. Zeek was so thoroughly frightened that he was scarcely able to stand and was terrorized into a confession. Zeek thought his time had come, and with a countenance ashy pale, related the circumstances of the killing as best he could. His confession was to the effect that he was an accomplice, and that Wagoner did the killing. After Beggs had been struck down, Mrs. Zeek (Zeek's wife) and a Mrs. Hall carried the body of the dead man from the scene to where it was afterward found. After Zeek's confession he was returned to his cell and locked up, evidently the mob desiring to keep him for further testimony respecting those whom he implicated. What Wagoner had to say in his last moments is not known. It is sufficient to know that in two minutes after he was taken from the jail he was suspended by the neck under a tree only a few feet from the court-house. The mob was very orderly in their work, being headed by a leader and all answering promptly to their numbers, showing that they had all been well drilled for the job in advance. Several belated citizens who happened to pass while the mob were carrying out their work, were halted by the guards stationed about and kept prisoners until the work was completed. The mob then quietly dispersed, going in all directions. The body of Wagoner was allowed to hang until morning when it was viewed and cut down by the Coroner and handed over to an undertaker. JUDGE LYNCH
Settles With John Wagoner.
IRONTON O., Jan. 21.—One night last November Dr. Josep Beggs was found about a mile from this town riddled with buckshot. The morning after his murder John Waggoner and Wm. Zeck were arrested, charged with the crime. A preliminary examination was held before Mayor Corns, and the two were committed without bail to answer the charge of murder in the first degree. Both Waggoner and Zeek were disreputable men, and belonged to disreputable families. The fact that two such degraded rascals had taken the life of so valuable a citizen as Dr. Beggs was enough aside from the terrible features surrounding the crime, to excite the community to a dangerous pitch of rage.

Threats of summary vengeance were heard on every side. The indignation was too intense to be smothered. Shortly after twelve o'clock last night Sheriff Kimball was aroused by a knocking at the jail door and getting up, went to answer it. No sooner did he open the door than, quick as a flash, he was seized by a band of masked men lying in wait outside, who told him that they didn't intend to hurt him, and ordered him to keep quiet. Before he could recover from his amazement three or four cocked revolvers were leveled at his head, and a stern, determined voice demanded of him the keys to the jail. The Sheriff, in his hurry to answer the knocking had come to the door in his undercloths, and of course did not have the keys with him. He was ordered to tell where they were. Being a men of grit he refused to do this. The talk so far had taken place in the hall, and then the masked gang some ten or fifteen in number marched him to the room that he had left, and renewed the demand. Again, a flat refusal. It looked as if the mob would be forced to beat down the doors or be baffled. But in this room was the Sheriff's wife. She, terrified by the midnight attack, the threats and the deadly looking revolvers, told the lynchers where the keys were. They unlocked the cell door, took Waggoner out into the Court House yard and hung him to the limb of a tree.

MARSHAL DAVID SNODGRASS, of Crestline, was shot and killed on the 21st. A man with no visible means of support had been hanging about town for several days, and the Marshal was watching him. While in a hardware store taking to Dr. Jenner, the man entered and asked to be shown some cartridges. The Marshal stepped up to the fellow and, after asking several questions about himself, asked him if he had a revolver. He replied that he had one at home. The Marshal then took hold of him, but the fellow tore away and ran, the Marshal and Dr. Jenner in hot pursuit. Before going four rods he turned and fired at the Marshal. Dr. Jenner then started in pursuit, hallooing "Catch that thief!" The pursued man then fired again, which struck the Marshal near the heart. Dr. Jenner, who was close behind the Marshal, saw the second shot had taken effect, and took Snodgrass into a drug-store, where he died in about seven minutes. The murderer was pursued by others, who by this time had joined in the chase, and finally captured and it was with great difficulty that the infuriated citizens were kept from lynching the fellow. Several persons however did take the trouble to hit the fellow over the head and beat and bruised him up considerable before he was gotten into the lockup.

saloon-murderer-logan.A1: A World correspondent visiting the Mormons has found a great deal to admire in their social life, and writes a flattering account of one of their settlements, called Logan, a place of four thousand inhabitants, where every man owns his farm, and where there are only two policemen, who have so little to do that they engage in other business. It is not because of their business. It is not because of their polygamous practices, however, that these Mormon settlers maintain good order without the intervention of the people. In fact the proportion of polygamists is very small. The population is select; in the first place, as to the sobriety, industry and thrifty habits of its members. Then, too, they have banished liquor from the settlement. When liquor was sold there a murder was committed in a drinking saloon, and these now orderly townfolks lynched the murderer and abolished the liquor traffic. After a time licenses were again issued, and there were soon ten times as many prisoners in tail as before the opening of saloons. The latter were then definitely closed, with the result that Logan cannot find full employment for its police force of two men. Polygamy, or the absence of it, has nothing whatever to do with this—in fact, there are other settlements, such as Vineland, where similarly good results were obtained; first, by the thrifty habits of the people, and next, by forbidding the sale of liquor.
